title: Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition: A Strong Batch-Normalization Statistics Baseline Under Cross-Water-Area Shift
content: Cross-water-area deployment can severely degrade underwater acoustic target-recognition (UATR) models, whereas conventional unsupervised domain adaptation often requires source recordings that may be unavailable in practice. We evaluate source-free, target-label-free adaptation on the two-class Oceanship–QiandaoEar22 protocol in both transfer directions. Using two independent five-seed batches (ten matched source checkpoints in total), we compare batch-normalization (BN) running-statistics re-estimation, entropy minimization (TENT), and a SHOT-style information-maximization implementation under a common evaluation pipeline directly comparable with source-data adaptation. Across the pooled ten-seed analysis, BN re-estimation attains the highest pooled mean macro-F1 of the three prespecified source-free baselines in both directions (0.5047 ocean-to-lake, 0.4900 lake-to-ocean), consistently improves over the unadapted source model, and outperforms TENT, while the lake-to-ocean ordering relative to SHOT-style adaptation remains unresolved. Controls indicate that the gain is associated with internal BN-statistics re-estimation rather than input renormalization or BN-affine entropy minimization. TENT can select confidently collapsed checkpoints under entropy-based label-free selection, whereas the SHOT-style implementation is sensitive to augmentation and class imbalance; an exploratory three-seed implementation of the original SHOT centroid pseudo-label mechanism approached bn_adapt, so conclusions about SHOT are restricted to the evaluated configurations. Source-data MMD achieved a higher mean macro-F1 in the initial lake-to-ocean batch, but this difference did not replicate and remained unresolved in the pooled ten-seed analysis. These results establish BN-statistics re-estimation as a strong low-overhead baseline for the evaluated source-free underwater acoustic adaptation setting, requiring only a single gradient-free pass over unlabeled target data. The conclusions are limited to one dataset pair, one BN-bearing architecture, a two-class shared label space, and the published segment-level split protocol, and do not establish independence at the recording or vessel level.
